Benchmarks

What the standard library costs and what the Scry taint checker finds, recorded as JSON and rendered here. Timings are environment-dependent: the same build on a different machine, kernel or load gives different absolute numbers. Compare two builds by interleaving them, not by comparing absolute times. Values that come from a single sample are labelled as such.

Generated by web/build-bench.py from the JSON in bench/ and scry/bench/. Every number is read from those files; the page is checked in so a stale rendering is a diff, and CI verifies that regenerating it is a no-op.

Standard library

The 18 hot paths recorded here, from lib/: maps, arrays, bytes, strings, sorting and hashing. Each mode does a fixed amount of work and prints a checksum, so a timing cannot be “fast” because the work disappeared.

A/B

A and B are the medians of the interleaved samples (one run of each build per sample, alternately first); the ratio is the median of the per-pair B/A ratios, so 1.000× means no change and a lower value is faster. The range is the slowest and fastest pair. Machine load cancels in a pair, but absolute times still depend on the machine.

Spread of each run

CV is the coefficient of variation of the samples inside one run: a property of the machine and its load, not of the change. “single run” means the file has one sample (or one repetition), so it records no variance at all; treat such a number as anecdotal.

Scry taint benchmark

The C taint corpus: for each case, the expected outcome is compared with the findings, and the ratios are computed in integer basis points so the file is stable. These are counts and detection rates, not timings. The baseline records no runtime for this run.

Paths in the file are relative to scry/. The case metrics are produced by the Scry checker’s bench command over the checked-in corpus manifest. The baseline records no date and no machine. Its git history is the only record of when it changed. It says nothing about the machine it ran on.

Overall

TP/FN/TN/FP are cases, not alerts; a case is a true positive only when every expected finding is matched with valid evidence. No variance is recorded: the analysis is deterministic, and each case is one run.

How to reproduce

The standard-library harness is checked in with its recorded data: it builds bench/stdlib-bench.wiz and runs each mode in its own process. The Scry figures are the Scry checker’s bench command over its corpus manifest; scry/bench/baseline.json is the baseline that run is compared with. 

# Standard library: build the A side (the compiler from the commit you compare
# against), then interleave it with the B side.
$OLD_WIZ build bench/stdlib-bench.wiz -o bench/.build/bench-base
scripts/stdlib-bench.py --bin bench/.build/bench-base --reps 15 \
    --json bench/stdlib-baseline.json
scripts/stdlib-bench.py --baseline-bin bench/.build/bench-base --reps 15 \
    --json bench/stdlib-bench.json

# A recorded run compared with a later run by medians (weaker: no pairing).
scripts/stdlib-bench.py --baseline bench/stdlib-baseline.json

# Scry taint corpus: metrics, not timing. Writes build/bench.json and .md.
cd scry && grail run scry -- bench --no-timing
cd scry && grail run scry -- bench --update-baseline bench/baseline.json

# Regenerate this page; CI runs the --check form, which must be a no-op.
python3 web/build-bench.py
python3 web/build-bench.py --check

Sizes are fixed in the benchmark program and passed to it, so a sample does exactly the work its JSON says. Nix users can run everything inside the development shell. Absolute times on a shared machine move by several percent; the paired ratios are the number to read.
